items.followUp: Define a chemical formula and explain how the formula for magnesium chloride (MgCl₂) is written using valencies.

rubric.why: Awards the definition of a chemical formula.
rubric.description: Defines a chemical formula as a symbolic representation showing the elements and number of atoms in a substance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, including what the symbols and numbers represent.

rubric.why: Checks the method for writing a formula.
rubric.description: Explains that element symbols are written and their valencies are used to determine the subscripts, usually by criss-crossing and simplifying if needed.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for explaining the use of symbols and valencies to obtain subscripts.

rubric.why: Checks application of the method with an example.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example showing how valencies give the formula.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a valid example with the relevant valencies or formula-writing step.

modelAnswer: A chemical formula is a symbolic representation of a substance that shows which elements are present and the number of atoms of each element.
Write the symbols of the elements, then use their valencies to determine the subscripts; criss-cross the valencies and simplify the ratio if necessary.
For example, aluminium has valency 3 and oxygen has valency 2.
Criss-crossing the valencies gives Al₂O₃, the formula of aluminium oxide.

items.followUp: Define an ionic compound and write three of its properties.

rubric.why: Checks the defining feature of covalent compounds.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent compound as one in which atoms are joined by sharing electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying electron sharing between atoms.

rubric.why: Checks a characteristic physical property.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either or both related low-temperature properties.

rubric.why: Checks electrical conductivity.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the electrical-conductivity property.

rubric.why: Checks solubility properties commonly given for covalent compounds.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds are generally insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the stated solubility pattern.

modelAnswer: A covalent compound is formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.
They are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.

items.followUp: State Bohr’s postulates about electron shells and explain what happens when an electron moves between shells.

rubric.why: Checks the postulate describing electron paths.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits or shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed electron paths around the nucleus.

rubric.why: Checks the energy of an orbit.
rubric.description: States that each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definite-energy postulate.

rubric.why: Checks the stability of electrons in permitted orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not radiate or lose energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that there is no energy loss in a stationary orbit.

rubric.why: Checks the energy change during transitions between orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it moves to a lower-energy orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each direction of energy transfer or 2 marks for clearly describing both.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits, called shells.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
An electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not radiate or lose energy.
An electron absorbs energy to move from a lower-energy orbit to a higher-energy orbit.
It emits energy when it moves from a higher-energy orbit to a lower-energy orbit.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature, surface area, humidity and wind speed affect the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature.
rubric.description: Explains that higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction and factor.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of exposed surface area.
rubric.description: Explains that a larger exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction and factor.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of humidity.
rubric.description: Explains that higher humidity slows evaporation, while lower humidity makes it faster.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between humidity and evaporation.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of moving air.
rubric.description: Explains that increased wind speed increases the rate of evaporation by carrying away vapour near the surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of wind speed.

modelAnswer: Higher temperature increases evaporation because more particles have enough energy to escape from the liquid.
A larger exposed surface area increases evaporation because more liquid particles can escape at the same time.
Higher humidity slows evaporation; low humidity makes evaporation faster.
Greater wind speed increases evaporation by carrying water vapour away from the liquid surface.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a true solution and a suspension, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks the defining feature of a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: States that a homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for uniform composition.

rubric.why: Checks the contrast and example for a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: States that a heterogeneous mixture is non-uniform and gives a suitable example; a suitable homogeneous-mixture example may also support the distinction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast with an example such as sand and water.

modelAnswer: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout; its components are evenly mixed, as in salt solution.
A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition, as in a mixture of sand and water.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of a sodium ion (Na⁺) in subshells.

rubric.why: Checks the complete subshell configuration of the chloride ion.
rubric.description: Gives the chloride ion’s 18-electron subshell configuration.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete correct configuration; award 1 mark for a substantially correct configuration with one subshell error or omission.

modelAnswer: A chloride ion, Cl⁻, has 18 electrons.
Its subshell electronic configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶.

items.followUp: Name two radioactive isotopes used in medicine and state what each is used to trace or examine.

rubric.why: Checks a medical isotope example and its application.
rubric.description: Names iodine-131 as an isotope used to examine or trace thyroid function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for iodine-131 with its thyroid application.

rubric.why: Checks a second medical isotope example and its application.
rubric.description: Names sodium-24 as an isotope used to trace blood circulation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for sodium-24 with its blood-circulation application.

modelAnswer: Iodine-131 is used as a tracer to examine the thyroid gland.
Sodium-24 is used as a tracer to study blood circulation.

items.followUp: Describe how shielding effect changes down a group and across a period, and give the reason for each trend.

rubric.why: Checks the trend in shielding effect down a group.
rubric.description: States that shielding effect increases down a group because the number of occupied inner shells increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct down-group trend.

rubric.why: Checks the trend across a period.
rubric.description: States that shielding effect remains nearly constant across a period because electrons are added to the same main shell and the number of inner shells is unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct across-period trend.

modelAnswer: Shielding effect increases down a group because each step adds an occupied electron shell.
Shielding effect remains nearly constant across a period because the number of inner shells does not change.
